name: Pashur the son of Immer
charge: Smiting the prophet and putting him in the stocks; prophesying lies
summary: Pashur, chief governor in the house of the Lord, heard Jeremiah prophesy the city's fall, struck him, and put him in the stocks at the high gate of Benjamin overnight. In the morning Jeremiah gave him a new name.
offense: Pashur, the priest and chief governor in the Lord's house, heard Jeremiah prophesy and struck him. He put the prophet in the stocks at the high gate of Benjamin, using his office to punish the word he should have received. When Pashur released him the next day, Jeremiah did not withdraw the message. The Lord gave Pashur the name Magor-missabib, fear round about. His violence against the messenger could neither disprove the prophecy nor remove the danger it announced.
judgment: The Lord declared that Pashur would become a terror to himself and his friends. Judah's strength and treasures would be given to Babylon. Pashur and his household would go into captivity, and he would die and be buried there with the friends to whom he had prophesied lies. The passage records this sentence against him; it does not give a separate account of its execution. The keeper of the stocks was warned of his own coming confinement. Authority in the sanctuary provided no exemption from answering for violence and false prophecy.

verses.text: Now Pashur the son of Immer the priest, who was also chief governor in the house of the Lord, heard that Jeremiah prophesied these things.
Then Pashur smote Jeremiah the prophet, and put him in the stocks that were in the high gate of Benjamin, which was by the house of the Lord.
And it came to pass on the morrow, that Pashur brought forth Jeremiah out of the stocks. Then said Jeremiah unto him, The Lord hath not called thy name Pashur, but Magor–missabib.

For thus saith the Lord, Behold, I will make thee a terror to thyself, and to all thy friends: and they shall fall by the sword of their enemies, and thine eyes shall behold it: and I will give all Judah into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he shall carry them captive into Babylon, and shall slay them with the sword.

Moreover I will deliver all the strength of this city, and all the labours thereof, and all the precious things thereof, and all the treasures of the kings of Judah will I give into the hand of their enemies, which shall spoil them, and take them, and carry them to Babylon.

And thou, Pashur, and all that dwell in thine house shall go into captivity: and thou shalt come to Babylon, and there thou shalt die, and shalt be buried there, thou, and all thy friends, to whom thou hast prophesied lies.
Then came Jeremiah from Tophet, whither the Lord had sent him to prophesy; and he stood in the court of the Lord’s house; and said to all the people,

Thus saith the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel; Behold, I will bring upon this city and upon all her towns all the evil that I have pronounced against it, because they have hardened their necks, that they might not hear my words.

Now it came to pass, when Jeremiah had made an end of speaking all that the Lord had commanded him to speak unto all the people, that the priests and the prophets and all the people took him, saying, Thou shalt surely die.

Why hast thou prophesied in the name of the Lord, saying, This house shall be like Shiloh, and this city shall be desolate without an inhabitant? And all the people were gathered against Jeremiah in the house of the Lord.
When the princes of Judah heard these things, then they came up from the king’s house unto the house of the Lord, and sat down in the entry of the new gate of the Lord’s house.
Then spake the priests and the prophets unto the princes and to all the people, saying, This man is worthy to die; for he hath prophesied against this city, as ye have heard with your ears.
If there be a controversy between men, and they come unto judgment, that the judges may judge them; then they shall justify the righteous, and condemn the wicked.
And it shall be, if the wicked man be worthy to be beaten, that the judge shall cause him to lie down, and to be beaten before his face, according to his fault, by a certain number.
Forty stripes he may give him, and not exceed: lest, if he should exceed, and beat him above these with many stripes, then thy brother should seem vile unto thee.

entries.commentary: Pashur the priest, chief governor in the house of the Most High, hears Jeremiah prophesy, smites him, and puts him in the stocks in the high gate of Benjamin. When he is let out the next day, Jeremiah tells him the Most High has renamed him Magor-missabib, a terror to himself and all his friends, for they shall fall by the sword of the king of Babylon. All Judah, all the strength and treasures of the city, and Pashur's whole household will be carried captive to Babylon, and Pashur will die there and be buried there with all the friends to whom he prophesied lies.

Jeremiah is going through it so bad, mocked and reproached daily, that he says he will not make mention of the Most High nor speak any more in His name. Just like us when we go out to camp, if somebody does not speak evil of us every time we do something big, there is a hater or somebody trying to demonize us. But the word was in his heart like a burning fire shut up in his bones; he was weary with holding it in and could not stay, he had to blast them, he could not hold it.

Jeremiah hears the defaming of many and his familiar friends watching for his stumbling, hoping to be enticed against him and take their revenge. The Most High is with him as a mighty terrible one, so his persecutors will stumble, not prevail, and be greatly ashamed in an everlasting confusion that will never be forgotten. He commits his cause to the Most High who tries the righteous and sees the reins and the heart, and sings praise because He delivers the soul of the poor from the hand of evildoers.

Crushed by the persecution, Jeremiah curses the day he was born and the man who brought his father the news of a man child, wishing that man to be like the cities the Most High overthrew. He asks why he came forth out of the womb only to see labor and sorrow and to have his days consumed with shame.

In the beginning of Jehoiakim's reign the Most High commands Jeremiah to stand in the court of the Lord's house and speak all His words to the cities of Judah, diminishing not a word, that they might hearken and turn from their evil way. If they will not hearken and walk in His law, He will make this house like Shiloh and this city a curse to all the nations of the earth.

When Jeremiah finished speaking all that the Most High commanded, the priests, the prophets, and all the people took him and said, Thou shalt surely die. They were angry that he prophesied the house would be like Shiloh and the city desolate; this is the same thing we go through when we read the Bible to people and tell them thus saith the Lord, and they get mad and want to harm us.

When the princes of Judah heard, they came up from the king's house and sat in the entry of the new gate, and the priests and prophets said this man is worthy to die for prophesying against this city. It was not about Jeremiah speaking the word of the Most High but about their feelings getting hurt; he prophesied only because the Most High told him what to say, the same way people today say you cannot speak against this country when we are only saying what the Bible says.

Jeremiah answers the princes and all the people that the Most High sent him to prophesy against this house and city, and tells them to amend their ways and obey, that the Most High might repent of the evil pronounced against them. He puts himself in their hand to do as they see good, but warns that if they put him to death they bring innocent blood upon themselves and upon the city, for of a truth the Most High sent him to speak these words.

The princes and all the people then say to the priests and prophets that this man is not worthy to die, for he has spoken in the name of the Most High; our people were rebellious but they were not that dumb. The elders rise and recall that Micah the Morasthite prophesied in the days of Hezekiah that Zion would be plowed like a field, yet Hezekiah did not put him to death but feared the Most High, who then repented of the evil.

The elders also recall Urijah the son of Shemaiah, who prophesied against the city like Jeremiah; when Jehoiakim sought to kill him he fled to Egypt, but the king sent men who fetched him back and slew him with the sword. One king knew the word came from the Most High and spared the prophet, while another king put his prophet to death; nevertheless the hand of Ahikam the son of Shaphan was with Jeremiah so he was not given to the people to be killed.

If there be a controversy between men, the judges justify the righteous and condemn the wicked; the wicked man worthy to be beaten was made to lie down and be beaten before the judge's face, according to his fault, by a certain number. Forty stripes may he give him, and not exceed, lest thy brother should seem vile unto thee. Paul recounted receiving that beating under this law.

Thou shalt not muzzle the ox when he treadeth out the corn: the corn is the reward for the ox. Paul applies this verse to how the elders are treated: let the elders that rule well be counted worthy of double honour, especially they who labour in the word and doctrine, for the labourer is worthy of his reward. Giving double honour is not just saying the words to the leadership; it is true respect and reverence toward the leadership that labours in this word and doctrine.

If brethren dwell together and one of them die and have no child, the wife of the dead was not to marry without unto a stranger; her husband's brother took her to wife, and the firstborn she bare succeeded in the name of the dead brother, that his name be not put out of Israel. Check this out: this is no longer the law, so do not try to use it as an excuse toward your brother's wife. It stood for the name not being put out because of the land inheritance in Israel. The man who refused was called before the elders; his brother's wife loosed his shoe from off his foot, spat in his face, and answered, So shall it be done unto that man that will not build up his brother's house; and his name was called in Israel, The house of him that hath his shoe loosed.

Remember what Amalek did unto thee by the way, when ye were come forth out of Egypt: he met thee by the way and smote the hindmost of thee, all that were feeble behind thee, when thou wast faint and weary, and he feared not God. Israel was later commanded through Samuel to repay it: I remember that which Amalek did to Israel; now go and smite Amalek, and utterly destroy all that they have, and spare them not. At Rephidim, where Amalek first came and fought with Israel, the Lord told Moses to write this for a memorial in a book and rehearse it in the ears of Joshua, for the Lord hath sworn that the Lord will have war with Amalek from generation to generation; and that war is still going on even to this day.
